articles.title: TAVR in Patients with Moderate Aortic Stenosis with At-Risk Features
articles.authors: Généreux P, Makkar RR, Pibarot P, Bax JJ, Lindman BR, Muhammad K, Oldemeyer JB, Pirwitz M, et al.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: For patients with moderate aortic stenosis, current guidelines recommend clinical surveillance with echocardiographic assessment every 1 or 2 years. Whether transcatheter aortic-valve replacement (TAVR) will improve outcomes in these patients remains unknown.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted an international, open-label, randomized trial to evaluate whether TAVR will result in better outcomes than clinical surveillance among patients with moderate aortic stenosis with at least one at-risk feature (i.e., a symptom or structural or functional abnormality that has been shown to be associated with faster disease progression or adverse cardiovascular outcomes). The patients were assigned in a 1:1 ratio to undergo transfemoral TAVR with a balloon-expandable valve or clinical surveillance. The primary effectiveness end point was a composite of death from any cause or a heart-failure event with or without hospitalization at 2 years. Superiority testing was performed in the intention-to-treat population.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 744 patients underwent randomization: 373 patients were assigned to the TAVR group and 371 to the clinical-surveillance group. The mean age of patients was 78 years, 39.1% were women, and 45.6% were at low surgical risk. The mean aortic-valve area was 1.2 cm2, and the mean aortic-valve peak velocity was 3.3 m per second. At 2 years, the Kaplan-Meier estimate of the percentage of patients with a primary effectiveness end-point event was 16.7% in the TAVR group and 23.9% in the clinical-surveillance group (risk difference, -7.2 percentage points; 95% confidence interval, -13.1 to -1.3; P = 0.02 for superiority). The Kaplan-Meier estimate of the percentage of patients who died from any cause was 8.4% in the TAVR group and 7.3% in the clinical-surveillance group; the estimates for a heart-failure event were 10.8% and 19.0%, respectively. The incidence of procedure-related adverse events did not differ meaningfully between the patients in the TAVR group and those in the clinical-surveillance group who underwent aortic-valve replacement.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Among patients with moderate aortic stenosis and at-risk features, a strategy of TAVR was superior to clinical surveillance in lowering the incidence of death or a heart-failure event at 2 years. (Funded by Edwards Lifesciences; PROGRESS ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04889872.).

articles.title: "It does feel different when you're seeing a colleague": A qualitative study of general practitioners' experiences of treating doctor-patients
articles.authors: Hettiarachchi D, Bradfield O, Tayal A, Bismark M

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Doctors have higher rates of burnout, suicide and substance use issues compared to the general profession and face numerous barriers to accessing medical care. Prior research has identified the need for improved guidance for treating doctors in caring for their doctor-patients.

abstract.label: AIM
abstract.text: Exploring GPs' experiences of caring for doctor-patients, we sought to identify insights to inform investment, policy and training initiatives to improve doctors' health.

abstract.label: DESIGN AND SETTING
abstract.text: A qualitative study involving 22 GPs in Australia.

abstract.label: METHOD
abstract.text: Semi-structured one-to-one interviews were transcribed and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Five themes emerged: (1) Barriers to doctor-patients seeking care are practical, professional, and psychological. (2) These barriers could be attenuated by adapting to doctor-patients' expertise and maintaining professional boundaries, while being thorough and clarifying expectations. (3) Mandatory reporting is rarely required and may support impaired doctors' recovery but can compromise the therapeutic alliance. (4) Nurturing a culture within the medical profession that values GP care and clearly defines the role of a regular GP, while normalising doctors' help-seeking can encourage doctors to engage with ongoing GP care. (5) Treating doctor-patients can be highly rewarding for GPs.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: As doctors face increasing complexity and challenges within their professional landscape, there is a need to prioritise doctors' health and encourage timely help-seeking. GPs are uniquely positioned to provide supportive care to their colleagues, and supportive infrastructure and cultural changes are needed to help GPs treat doctor-patients effectively and navigate medicolegal complexities.

articles.title: Difficulties with early prostate cancer diagnosis: a multi-perspective mixed-methods study
articles.authors: Hiscock J, Formby L, Din N, Hendry A, Wilkinson CE

abstract.text: Background Despite progress in treatment, the early stages of diagnosing prostate cancer remain difficult to navigate. GPs often work with vague symptoms and imperfect tests without a routine screening programme. Understanding how patients, GPs, and secondary care urologists experience the diagnostic process is important to inform efforts to improve pathways and reduce delays. Aim The aim was to map the timing and sequence of key events in men's initial diagnostic journeys, explore decision-making of patients, GPs, and urologists, and identify points where earlier or more equitable diagnosis might be supported. Design & Setting A mixed-methods study conducted in Wales, UK, combining descriptive questionnaire data with thematic qualitative interviews and focus groups. Method Questionnaire data from 210 patients, 65 GPs, and 69 urologists were analysed descriptively. Qualitative interviews and focus groups with patients (n = 24), GPs (n = 18), and secondary care clinicians (n = 11) were analysed thematically. Results Patients described symptom recognition delays, and multiple barriers to diagnosis including accessing appointments, repeat presentations, and diagnostic test waits. GPs highlighted challenges in managing uncertainty and variation in access to investigations. Urologists described limitations in resources and referral pathways. All described delays were shaped by wider systemic factors as well as primary care processes. Conclusion Delays in prostate cancer diagnosis stem not only from primary care, but also from system-wide challenges. Consistent pathways and improved access to diagnostic tests may reduce variation and delays. Understanding men's experiences and journeys to diagnosis will inform service improvement.

articles.title: Are non-cancer diagnoses missed opportunities in diagnosing cancer? Observational case-control studies
articles.authors: Price S, Abel GA, Black G, Friedemann Smith C, Hamilton W, King A, Laity G, Lavu D, et al.

abstract.text: Background Initial non-cancer diagnoses that plausibly explain cancer symptoms may be underexplored missed opportunities in cancer diagnosis. Aim To characterise "interim diagnoses" representing potential missed opportunities to diagnose cancer; namely, non-cancer conditions diagnosed before cancer that are associated both with cancer and better and/or worse cancer outcomes. Design and Setting Observational case-control and case-only analyses of registry-linked Clinical Practice Research Datalink data from English primary care. Methods Cancer cases (cancer registry diagnoses, 1/1/2012-31/12/2018) were matched to cancer-free controls on birth year, gender and general practice. Incident non-cancer diagnoses sharing cancer symptoms were sought in the year before the case's diagnosis. Conditional logistic regression characterised non-cancer diagnoses associated with cancer (Bonferroni-corrected p<0.05). Associations between non-cancer diagnoses and cancer outcomes were tested using logistic regression (stage, route to diagnosis) and parametric regression accelerated failure-time models (1-year survival). Results Analyses of 223,422 patients yielded evidence of 37 "interim diagnoses" across 7 cancer sites that were consistently associated with worse (n=18) or better (n=8) cancer outcomes, or a mixture of worse and better outcomes within or between cancer sites (n=11). For example, gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, gastritis, oesophagitis, or peptic ulcer were associated with worse outcomes in pancreatic, colorectal and ovarian cancers, with better outcomes in stomach cancer, and a mixture in oesophageal cancer. Conclusion We characterise 37 "interim" diagnoses as potential missed opportunities in cancer diagnosis. Safety-netting around these non-cancer diagnoses, focussing on management of clinical uncertainty and robust patient follow-up, may help avoid missed opportunities to diagnose cancer and improve outcomes.

articles.title: Molecular bacterial detection in nasopharyngeal swabs does not predict the clinical course of lower respiratory tract infections in primary care: an ancillary study of a randomized controlled trial
articles.authors: Knüsli J, Lhopitallier L, Kronenberg A, Perrenoud MA, Page MA, Mamin A, D'Acremont V, Senn N, et al.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Point-of-care molecular tests on easily collected samples could support antimicrobial stewardship in primary care.

abstract.label: AIM
abstract.text: To determine whether molecular bacterial detection in nasopharyngeal swabs is associated with a worse disease course in patients with lower respiratory tract infections (LRTIs).

abstract.label: DESIGN AND SETTING
abstract.text: Secondary analysis of a randomized controlled trial including 469 consecutive patients with LRTI, from 60 primary care practices in Switzerland.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Polymerase chain reaction assays for respiratory viruses and bacteria were retrospectively performed on nasopharyngeal swabs. Kaplan-Meier analyses and a multivariate Cox regression were used to evaluate time to recovery according to bacterial detection.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 345 patients were included, of which 142 (41%) had bacteria detected. The detection of bacteria did not influence median time to recovery (7 days in both groups, 95% confidence interval [CI] 6-8 days, p=0.29). Bacterial detection was not associated with time to recovery (adjusted hazard ratio 1.13, 95% CI 0.84-1.50, p=0.42), nor was the interaction term between bacterial detection and antibiotic prescription (adjusted hazard ratio 1.10, 95% CI 0.64-1.90, p=0.74), indicating independence from antibiotic treatment. The detection of bacteria was not associated with a different median duration of cough, sputum, or dyspnoea. The median duration of cough of any severity was 16 days (95% CI 15-18 days).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Among patients with LRTI in primary care, molecular detection of bacteria in nasopharyngeal swabs did not predict a worse disease course. These findings cast doubts on the utility of syndromic molecular testing for managing LRTIs in this setting.

articles.title: Why primary care clinicians use advice and guidance: a qualitative study
articles.authors: Faux-Nightingale A, Harrison R, Burton C, Bajpai R, Clarson LE, Hadley-Barrows T, Haines J, Helliwell T, et al.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Where available, advice and guidance (A&G) can enable primary care clinicians to seek specialist input, supporting decision making and avoiding unnecessary referrals. The use of A&G has significantly expanded, accelerated by COVID-19 and contractual changes. Although A&G is intended to streamline elective care, concerns persist regarding workload shift, variable responsiveness, and system usability. Despite growing policy emphasis, little is known about why clinicians choose to use A&G.

abstract.label: AIM
abstract.text: To explore the current use of A&G within primary care, focusing on decision-making processes that underpin primary care clinicians' decisions to use A&G.

abstract.label: DESIGN AND SETTING
abstract.text: Qualitative study set in English primary care.

abstract.label: METHOD
abstract.text: Twenty semi-structured video interviews were conducted with primary care clinicians purposively sampled for maximum variation. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis within an interpretive description framework, with themes developed collaboratively and refined through discussion with researchers and patient and public involvement and engagement contributors.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Four overarching themes encapsulate clinicians' decisions to use A&G: clinical presentation (acuity and complexity), navigating healthcare pathways, previous experiences of A&G, and using A&G to validate clinical decision making. Barriers included delayed responses and uncertainty about inequitable workload distribution. These factors shape how effectively A&G could be integrated into routine practice.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Primary care clinicians use A&G to support patient care and aid decision making, but its effectiveness depends on timely, clinically helpful responses. Ensuring responses remain appropriate to primary care remit and capacity will be essential if A&G becomes the main route into elective care.

articles.title: GP roles in emergency ambulance services in the UK: a qualitative realist study
articles.authors: Burrell A, Booker M

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Demand on emergency healthcare services is increasing. Utilising GPs in emergency ambulance services (EASs) may be effective at reducing avoidable conveyances to emergency departments and releasing emergency ambulances for high-acuity cases. There is limited evidence on models of GP EAS roles in the UK.

abstract.label: AIMS
abstract.text: To describe the current provision of GP EAS roles and to develop a provisional explanatory programme theory.

abstract.label: DESIGN & SETTING
abstract.text: Qualitative realist interview study involving professionals with detailed knowledge and experience of GPs working in EASs across the UK.

abstract.label: METHOD
abstract.text: Potential participants were identified and approached by research and development teams at ambulance trusts. Interviews were semi-structured, with questions developed, piloted, and refined by the research team. Interviews were conducted online with 27 participants, with a realist approach taken to data analysis to explore the mechanisms by which GP EAS roles produce their intended outcomes in different contexts.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The GP role is predominantly to undertake enhanced remote patient assessment following an initial algorithmic triage, aiming to provide the most appropriate level of care. While optimising the clinical response to individual callers, this also serves a system-level function by protecting ambulance resources to support timely responses to high-acuity patients. The mechanism behind GP triage was explored through existing middle-range theories around risk individualisation - the process of translating organisational risk appetite to individual patient contacts. This helps the ambulance service to make 'braver' decisions, namely, those involving non-conveyance, alternatives to conveyance, or lower-acuity responses. GPs do this effectively due to their seniority, broad clinical knowledge and experience, approach to risk and uncertainty, ability to practise outside guidelines, consultation and communication skills, and system awareness.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: GPs in EASs serve both individual patients and the system by individualising organisational approaches to risk and resource management.

articles.title: Impact of an initial non-cancer diagnosis before a subsequent cancer diagnosis: a secondary qualitative analysis of patient perspectives in the UK
articles.authors: Ramasawmy M, Abel G, Bell Black G, Friedemann Smith C, Hamilton W, King A, Neal RD, Nicholson BD, et al.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Timely diagnosis of cancer can be challenging as most individuals present with non-specific symptoms in primary care. One-third of those diagnosed with cancer report receiving a non-cancer diagnosis, before being referred for cancer investigations ('interim' diagnosis), presenting a potential missed diagnostic opportunity.

abstract.label: AIM
abstract.text: This study explores patients' experiences of receiving a non-cancer diagnosis before referral for suspected cancer investigation.

abstract.label: DESIGN AND SETTING
abstract.text: Secondary qualitative analysis of seven interview datasets collected in UK primary care since 2015.

abstract.label: METHOD
abstract.text: Patient journeys were summarised, charted, and analysed using framework analysis. Patient Public Involvement and Engagement collaborators were involved throughout.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of n = 58 transcripts in which patients presented to primary care with symptoms and received an interim non-cancer diagnosis were included in the study. We identified eight common scenarios involving an initial non-cancer diagnosis followed by referral for suspected cancer. For example, individuals considered at low risk of cancer reported symptoms being linked to lifestyle factors, and required multiple contacts over time before further investigation was considered. Patients queried interim diagnoses when they felt their symptoms and interpretations had been poorly understood, or they had been given inappropriate investigations or ineffective treatment. While patients recognised the difficulty of deciding when common symptoms required onward referral, they trusted clinicians who were responsive to their concerns, regardless of outcome.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Interim diagnoses arise as part of the normal diagnostic process in patients presenting with non-specific symptoms. Challenging these diagnoses in the face of new evidence could mitigate potential delays in diagnosis and improve patient outcomes.

articles.title: Evaluating additional roles in primary care: expanding capacity and transforming care delivery
articles.authors: Hong J, Penfold C, Edwards PJ, Kashyap MN, Mcleod H, Salisbury C, Walsh N, Bennett B, et al.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: The Additional Roles Reimbursement Scheme (ARRS), introduced by NHS England in 2019, aimed to expand the workforce, promote multidisciplinary team-based care, and improve patient outcomes.

abstract.label: AIM
abstract.text: To examine changes in consultation rates and outcomes in relation to ARRS implementation, and compare outcomes across primary care roles.

abstract.label: DESIGN AND SETTING
abstract.text: Longitudinal cohort study using the Clinical Practice Research Datalink (CPRD) AURUM, analysing 12 170 079 consultations (2015-2021) from 600 000 randomly sampled patients at 400 English practices.

abstract.label: METHOD
abstract.text: Joinpoint regression modelled trends in age- and sex-standardised consultation rates, further consultations within 1-14 days, prescribing, and referrals. Multilevel regression compared outcomes between diagnostic-capable roles and GPs.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Most consultations remained GP- or nurse-led, but rates with direct patient care (DPC)-ARRS-eligible roles increased, particularly for pharmacists, physiotherapists, and nursing associates. For paramedics and mental health practitioners, growth preceded formal ARRS inclusion, suggesting the scheme accelerated rather than initiated expansion. Most DPC-ARRS-eligible roles were consulted more frequently in less deprived areas, except physiotherapists. Compared with GPs, most DPC-ARRS-eligible roles delivered more consultations face to face (except pharmacists), had lower prescribing (except advanced nurse practitioners) and referral rates, and higher further consultation rates with a diagnostic-capable clinician within 1-14 days (except pharmacists). However, all DPC-ARRS-eligible roles had lower odds of a further consultation specifically with a GP.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: ARRS has supported and accelerated the diversification of the primary care skill mix. Patterns of consultation activity suggest an expansion of overall primary care capacity with some redistribution of workload across the multidisciplinary team, rather than a direct reduction in GP workload.

articles.title: Enriching New-onset Diabetes for Pancreatic Cancer (ENDPAC): external validation using English sentinel network
articles.authors: Price CA, Claridge H, de Lusignan S, Khalaf N, Mold F, Smith NA, Winn M, Lemanska A

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Pancreatic cancer has a very low survival rate due to late diagnosis. Symptoms are often non-specific, thereby complicating early detection in primary care. The Enriching New-onset Diabetes for Pancreatic Cancer (ENDPAC) algorithm uses weight change, glycaemic control, and age at diabetes onset to identify patients with new-onset diabetes (NOD) who are at increased risk of pancreatic cancer. It was developed in the US and has not been validated in the UK.

abstract.label: AIM
abstract.text: To validate ENDPAC in a UK primary care population and assess its predictive utility.

abstract.label: DESIGN & SETTING
abstract.text: Retrospective cohort study using ORCHID, a national primary care sentinel network.

abstract.label: METHOD
abstract.text: Adults aged ≥50 years with NOD, requisite glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c), and weight data were included. ENDPAC scores were calculated and model performance was evaluated via discrimination, calibration, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV). The Youden index identified optimal cut-offs. Sensitivity analyses were used to assess measurement timing, repeat HbA1c testing, and multiple values.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 70 050 individuals, 185 (0.26%) developed pancreatic cancer. These people were older, and had higher HbA1c and greater weight-loss levels at diagnosis than those who did not develop pancreatic cancer. ENDPAC achieved an area under the curve of 0.734. An optimal ENDPAC score cut-off of ≥3 classified 27.8% of individuals as high risk, with 62.6% sensitivity, 72.5% specificity, 0.6% PPV, and 99.9% NPV. Sensitivity analyses showed similar performance across measurement windows and handling of multiple values.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: ENDPAC shows moderate discrimination in UK primary care. Although it had a relatively low PPV, integration into routine systems as part of a sequential diagnostic pathway could provide scalable, low-cost, automated risk stratification, thereby identifying people with NOD who are at a higher risk of developing pancreatic cancer.

articles.title: Coronary CT Angiography versus Intravascular Ultrasound Guidance for PCI
articles.authors: Collet C, Mizukami T, Bouisset F, Pontone G, Zivelonghi C, Jones DA, Wilgenhof A, Støttrup NB, et al.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Intravascular ultrasound (IVUS)-guided percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) improves clinical outcomes. Coronary computed tomographic angiography (CCTA) provides anatomical and physiological information before cardiac catheterization that may enable PCI planning. Data regarding the use of CCTA-guided PCI as compared with IVUS-guided PCI with respect to clinical outcomes are lacking.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: In this investigator-initiated, international, open-label, randomized, noninferiority trial with blinded end-point adjudication, we randomly assigned patients with a clinical indication for revascularization, at least one epicardial lesion with a diameter stenosis of more than 70%, and a fractional flow reserve derived from CCTA of 0.80 or less in a 1:1 ratio to a CCTA-guided or IVUS-guided PCI strategy. The primary end point was target-vessel failure, defined as a composite of death from cardiac causes, target-vessel myocardial infarction, or ischemia-driven target-vessel revascularization, at 12 months. The noninferiority margin for the absolute risk difference was 4.5 percentage points, with a prespecified hierarchical testing strategy for superiority.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 1105 patients underwent randomization: 556 to the CCTA-guided PCI group and 549 to the IVUS-guided PCI group. The median age of the patients was 65 years, and 21.7% were women. At 12 months, target-vessel failure had occurred in 23 patients (4.1%) in the CCTA-guided PCI group and in 25 patients (4.6%) in the IVUS-guided PCI group (risk difference, -0.42 percentage points; 95% confidence interval, -2.82 to 1.99; P<0.001 for noninferiority; P = 0.73 for superiority). A total of 6 patients in the CCTA-guided PCI group and 9 patients in the IVUS-guided PCI group had clinical procedural complications.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: A CCTA-guided PCI strategy was noninferior to IVUS-guided PCI with respect to target-vessel failure at 12 months. (Funded by GE HealthCare and Heartflow; P4 ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT05253677.).

articles.title: Experience and impacts of violence and abuse by patients and the public towards general practice staff: a qualitative study
articles.authors: Chou S, Tyrrell E, Rowe E, Bryant J

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: General practice (family medicine) experiences more violence and abuse by patients and the public than in general hospital settings. Qualitative accounts on how violence and abuse are experienced and perceived remain limited in both breadth and depth.

articles.title: Laparoscopic Versus Open Liver Resection for Colorectal Liver Metastases : An Individual Participant Data Meta-analysis of Four Randomized Clinical Trials
articles.authors: Olij B, Pilz da Cunha G, Pugh SA, Abu Hilal M, Lopez-Lopez V, Aghayan D, Brusadin R, Fichtinger RS, et al.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Randomized clinical trials (RCTs) have compared laparoscopic liver resection (LLR) and open liver resection (OLR) for colorectal liver metastases (CRLM); however, long-term outcomes and subgroup effects have not been comprehensively evaluated.

abstract.label: PURPOSE
abstract.text: To compare postoperative and long-term oncologic outcomes after LLR versus OLR for CRLM using individual participant data from RCTs.

abstract.label: DATA SOURCES
abstract.text: PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials were searched from database inception through March 2025 for RCTs comparing LLR and OLR for CRLM.

abstract.label: STUDY SELECTION
abstract.text: Eligible studies were RCTs comparing LLR and OLR for CRLM.

abstract.label: DATA EXTRACTION
abstract.text: Individual participant data, including unpublished data, were obtained from trial investigators of all 4 published RCTs.

abstract.label: DATA SYNTHESIS
abstract.text: Analyses used a modified intention-to-treat approach and 1-stage individual participant data meta-analysis (IPDMA) with trial-adjusted regression models and g-computation to estimate standardized treatment effects across outcomes, with 95% CIs obtained by nonparametric bootstrap resampling. Prespecified subgroup analyses assessed heterogeneity of treatment effect for the primary outcome. A total of 761 patients were included (laparoscopic, n = 384; open, n = 377). Postoperative morbidity was lower in patients assigned to laparoscopic surgery compared with open surgery (19% vs. 27%). Among patients who received preoperative systemic therapy, morbidity did not differ between groups (25% vs. 24%). Ninety-day mortality was 1.8% after LLR and 0.8% after OLR. After a median follow-up of 93 months, overall survival and disease-free survival did not differ between groups.

abstract.label: LIMITATION
abstract.text: Analyses were limited to variables available across all studies.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: In this IPDMA of all published RCTs in the field, LLR for CRLM was associated with lower postoperative morbidity than OLR, with similar long-term oncologic outcomes.

abstract.text: None. (PROSPERO: CRD42024502655).

articles.title: Obesity and Cancer Risk in Young Adults in Korea : A Nationwide Health Screening Cohort Study
articles.authors: Yun JS, Mun H, Jung JH, Park Y, Kim SY, Kim K, Ko SH, Ahn YB, et al.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Obesity and early-onset cancer are both increasing among young adults, yet evidence remains limited.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To assess associations between obesity and early-onset cancer risk in young adults.

abstract.label: DESIGN
abstract.text: Nationwide population-based cohort study.

abstract.label: SETTING
abstract.text: Korean National Health Insurance Service database, 2009 to 2021.

abstract.label: PATIENTS
abstract.text: 6 313 338 adults aged 20 to 39 years without prior cancer, from a national health screening program.

abstract.label: MEASUREMENTS
abstract.text: Body mass index (BMI) was categorized into 5 groups (underweight to class II obesity) according to Asian-specific criteria. The outcome was incident cancer.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: During a mean follow-up of 11.2 years, 151 893 cancer cases occurred. Ten-year cumulative incidence ranged from 1.84% (95% CI, 1.83% to 1.86%) in the normal-weight group to 2.24% (CI, 2.22% to 2.27%) in class I obesity and 2.62% (CI, 2.56% to 2.68%) in class II obesity, with absolute risk differences of 0.40% (CI, 0.39% to 0.41%) and 0.78% (CI, 0.73% to 0.82%). The relative association was more pronounced in men, and absolute risk differences were greater in women. In combined BMI-waist circumference analyses, people with class I obesity based on BMI and with abdominal obesity had higher 10-year cumulative incidence (2.45% [CI, 2.41% to 2.50%]) than those without abdominal obesity (2.13% [CI, 2.10% to 2.16%]), exceeding that of those with class II obesity without abdominal obesity (2.20% [CI, 2.03% to 2.36%]). The highest cumulative incidence was observed for thyroid, endometrial, and ovarian cancer. Obesity was not associated with higher risk for breast cancer diagnosed by age 50 years.

abstract.label: LIMITATIONS
abstract.text: Observational design; nonrepresentative sample limited to screening participants; and unmeasured confounding, including smoking burden.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Obesity in young Korean adults, measured by BMI and waist circumference, is associated with higher early-onset cancer risk persisting into midlife, with patterns varying by cancer type. Early weight management may be important for prevention.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The rate of LLM-recommended overuse was 5.4% (95% CI, 0.6% to 12.2%); LLMs did not recommend overuse in 8 of 15 recommendations. Two recommendations accounted for most LLM-recommended overuse: thyroid ultrasound for an incidental subcentimeter nodule (overuse recommended in 42.8% of LLM responses) and routine electrocardiography in low-risk adults (overuse recommended in 28.3% of LLM responses). The LLMs recommended overuse in 0.6% to 3.3% of responses for the remaining 5 recommendations. False restraint was rare (0.6% [CI, 0.1% to 1.2%]), was absent for 11 of 15 recommendations, and was highest for prostate-specific antigen screening (3.3%).
abstract.textZh: LLM建議過度使用率為5.4% （ 95% CI ， 0.6%至12.2% ） ； 15項建議中有8項LLM不建議過度使用。兩項建議解釋了大多數LLM建議過度使用的原因：針對附帶的次公分結節進行甲狀腺超聲檢查（ 42.8%的LLM回應中建議過度使用） ，以及針對低風險成人進行常規心電圖檢查（ 28.3%的LLM回應中建議過度使用）。LLM建議過度使用，其餘5項建議的回應為0.6%至3.3%。錯誤限制很少見（ 0.6% [CI ， 0.1%至1.2%] ） ， 15項建議中有11項不存在，前列腺特異性抗原篩選最高（ 3.3% ）。

abstract.label: LIMITATIONS
abstract.text: Single prompts without follow-up; a benchmark rather than real-world use; responses classified by LLM judge with physician adjudication. Findings may not extend to consumer-facing use.
abstract.textZh: 沒有追蹤的單次提示；基準而非實際使用；由LLM法官歸類並由醫生裁定的回應。調查結果可能無法延伸至面向消費者的使用。

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: The LLMs rarely withheld recommendations for treatment when it was appropriate. Overuse was concentrated in 2 recommendations.
abstract.textZh: 法學碩士很少在適當的時候隱瞞治療建議。過度使用集中在2個建議。
